summary.title: Tips on naming boolean variables - Cleaner Code
summary.one_liner: Practical rules for naming boolean variables in JavaScript, such as matching names to every()/some() and avoiding negative or custom prefixes.
keywords: how to name a boolean in code
takeaways: Use is/has prefixes for booleans by default, but check edge cases where the convention reads badly.
Name every()-based booleans like isEveryUserOnline and some()-based ones like isAnyUserActive or isSomeUserActive.
Avoid numeric words like isOneUserActive, which can imply a count that isn't true.
Prefer affirmative names (isEnabled, isActive) over negative ones (isDisabled, isNotActive) to avoid double negatives like !isDisabled.
Restructuring a negated some() check into an every() check can make the condition easier to read.
summary.summary: The article reviews common edge cases in naming boolean variables and functions beyond the usual is/has prefix convention. It walks through booleans built from Array.every and Array.some, with tables rating candidate names for grammar, ambiguity and readability. It then covers avoiding custom prefixes like wasPaidFor, preferring affirmative names over negative ones, and rewriting a negated some() check as an every() check. The author notes that rules have exceptions and that the list is not exhaustive.
